definition: Calmness and an even temper, especially when facing stress, setbacks or bad news.
example: Years of mountain hiking taught him to meet sudden storms with equanimity rather than alarm.
nuance: Equanimity is steady balance kept under strain, while serenity can describe calm when nothing is troubling you at all.
prompt: A chess player loses her queen early in an important tournament game.
options: She absorbed the loss with equanimity and quietly planned her next defense.
Her equanimity showed as she slammed the board and stormed out of the hall.
She demanded equanimity, insisting the prize money be split evenly among all players.
Out of equanimity, she stopped caring about the match and stared at the ceiling.
reasons: Staying steady and thinking clearly after a setback is exactly this kind of calm.
Slamming things and storming off show a lost temper, the reverse of an even mind.
The word refers to an even temper, not an even division of money.
Calm under pressure is different from giving up interest, which is apathy.

practice.prompt: A baker's oven breaks an hour before a large catering order is due.
options: With equanimity, the baker phoned a neighbor who had a spare oven and kept working.
The baker's equanimity made him pace frantically and shout at his assistants.
The baker used equanimity to divide the dough into twelve loaves of identical weight.
The baker felt such equanimity about the order that he went home and left it unfinished.
reasons: Handling a sudden crisis calmly and practically shows a steady temper.
Frantic pacing and shouting reveal panic, not a composed state of mind.
This mixes up the word with equal measurement; it describes mood, not portions.
Abandoning the work shows indifference, which is not the same as staying calm.
